# Basic dashboards

Now that you know the basic features of the dashboards app, it’s time to create your first dashboard!

For that, [create a new dashboard](/ui/apps/dynatrace.dashboards) and call it “\<your name\> Kubernetes Overview”

## Metrics Exercise
For the first dashboard tile, we’d like to see an overview of the CPU usage of your Kubernetes pods as a pie chart.

In order to get that, add a new Metric to your dashboard:


![](data:image/jpeg;base64,)

And select the “Kubernetes: Container – CPU usage” metric:

![](data:image/jpeg;base64,)

* Filter for the `k8s.namespace.name` = “easytrade” - this will give you only the records for the “easytrade” namespace.
* Split the metric by the `k8s.pod.name`. This represents a pod in Dynatrace.
> **Pro tip**: splitting your metrics by anything called `dt.entity.*` will allow you to do drilldowns to other Dynatrace Apps later on. The corresponding entity to a pod name is `dt.entity.cloud_application_instance`, for the Kubernetes workload it’s `dt.entity.cloud_application`. You can find a list of all entities in the [Dynatrace semantic dictionary](https://docs.dynatrace.com/docs/discover-dynatrace/references/semantic-dictionary/model/dt-entities#cloud-application-instance).
* Add “Reduce to single value” and select “Avg” for it. This will allow you use a single value rather than a whole timeseries.
* Add a “Sort” and sort by `avg(dt.kubernetes.container.cpu_usage)`- this will sort the values in the right order.
* Remove the limit – we want to see all values!

Once you have done all of this, your explore metrics should look like this:

input.value:
timeseries { avg(dt.kubernetes.container.cpu_usage), value.A = avg(dt.kubernetes.container.cpu_usage, scalar: true) }, by: { k8s.pod.name, dt.entity.cloud_application_instance, dt.entity.cloud_application, dt.entity.cloud_application_namespace }, filter: { matchesValue(k8s.namespace.name, "otel-demo") }
| fieldsAdd dt.entity.cloud_application_instance.name = entityName(dt.entity.cloud_application_instance)
| fieldsAdd dt.entity.cloud_application.name = entityName(dt.entity.cloud_application)
| fieldsAdd dt.entity.cloud_application_namespace.name = entityName(dt.entity.cloud_application_namespace)
| sort `avg(dt.kubernetes.container.cpu_usage)` desc

## Duplicating charts and chart interactions

It often makes sense to chart the same data in multiple ways to make them better understandable. 
On the top of your chart, click the “Duplicate” button. 
* Remove the “Reduce to single value” and select “Line” in the visuals. 
* Rearrange your charts in whatever way you’d like. 

As a result, your dashboard should now look like this:

![](data:image/jpeg;base64,)

Dashboards allow us to interact with them in many ways. When you hover over them, you will see an interaction pane: 

![](data:image/jpeg;base64,)

With the default selection of “Explore”, you can zoom into a timeseries chart by selecting a specific time. As a result, the timeframe of the whole dashboard will be updated and the other charts are reloaded. 

![](data:image/jpeg;base64,)

In “Pan”, you can move backward and forward in time. Again, this will be applied to the whole dashboard.

The “Zoom in” and “Zoom out” buttons allow you to further drill into a specific timeframe.

Once you’re done, you can reset the timeframe by clicking on reset: 

![](data:image/jpeg;base64,)

You can also have a look at a single timeseries to analyze that one further by clicking on the timeseries name in the legend, or hide a single timeseries by clicking on the color next to it. 

![](data:image/jpeg;base64,)

Last but not least, you can also drill into other applications from a dashboard by selecting the three little dots and selecting “Open Record with…”
![](data:image/jpeg;base64,)

This will open a list of applications that you can drill down to:

![](data:image/jpeg;base64,)

## Logs tile

As a next step, we want to display all logs in our easytrade namespace that have the word “exception” in them. 

In order to do that, add a new “Logs” tile to the dashboard. 
* In the filter, filter by `k8s.namespace.name` = otel-demo AND `content` = \*exception\*
> The asterisks in \*exception\* makes sure that you search for this expression within the content.
* Sort by the timeframe – descending. Once you have done that, your filter should look like this:

input.value:
fetch logs
| filter matchesValue(k8s.namespace.name, "otel-demo") AND matchesValue(content, "*exception*")
| sort timestamp desc
| limit 20

Now it’s time to fix the visuals!

* In the visuals tab, in Columns, only select timestamp, status and content as the columns.
* Enable Line wrap and monospaced font for the “content” field.
Once you’re done, your visuals tab should look like this:

![](data:image/jpeg;base64,)

## Working with Thresholds

In Dashboards, you can put thresholds and coloring both on numerical values as well as strings. 
Add a new threshold to the log table, on the field “status”. For yellow, select “WARN”. For red, select “ERROR” as the value of your threshold:

![](data:image/jpeg;base64,)

You also have options to make these thresholds even more visual – in the “Cells” section, you can select “Apply threshold color to Background”. To even show this for the whole row, you can also tick “show threshold in row”.

The resulting table should look like this:

## Exploring events

Now, we’d like to see all Kubernetes events from the easytrade namespace on our dashboard.

For this, add a new “Event” tile to the dashboard. In the filter, select `event.provider`=”KUBERNETES_EVENT” and `k8s.namespace.name`=”easytrade”.

Now, convert this to timeseries and specify the count, split by dt.kubernetes.event.reason.

![](data:image/jpeg;base64,)

Once that is done, it’s time to check the visuals again. This time, select a bar chart for visualization.

The resulting chart should look like this (Hint: if you don’t have data, try selecting a longer timeframe.)

grail.canonicalQuery:
fetch events
| filter matchesValue(k8s.namespace.name, "easytrade") AND matchesValue(event.provider, "KUBERNETES_EVENT")
| makeTimeseries by:{dt.kubernetes.event.reason}, count = count()

sections.markdown:
## Forecasts

Forecasting data using Davis AI can be a powerful way of using Dynatrace for things like capacity planning and others.

In this example, we want to use Dynatrace to forecast the needed memory for our Kubernetes workloads.

Add a new metric tile for `dt.kubernetes.container.memory_working_set`. Filter by the `k8s.namespace.name`=”easytrade” and split by `k8s.workload.name`:

![](data:image/jpeg;base64,)

Forecasts work best on a longer period of data. Select a custom timeframe of “Last 30 days”.

![](data:image/jpeg;base64,)

Now, go to the “Davis AI” section, enable Davis, and use the “Forecast” analyzer. Click on “Run”.

![](data:image/jpeg;base64,)

In Visuals, select the “Davis AI Analysis” chart. For the visible selections, select “Chart”.

The resulting chart should look like this:

input.value:
timeseries { avg(dt.kubernetes.container.memory_working_set), value.A = avg(dt.kubernetes.container.memory_working_set, scalar: true) }, by: { k8s.workload.name }, filter: { matchesValue(k8s.namespace.name, "easytrade") }
| limit 20

grail.canonicalQuery:
timeseries by:{k8s.workload.name}, filter:matchesValue(k8s.namespace.name, "easytrade"), avg(dt.kubernetes.container.memory_working_set)
